items.stem: Which is an example of indirect characterisation?
options: "He looked at his shoes when I waved."
"He was a kind boy."
"He was embarrassed."
"She was very shy."
items.answer: "He looked at his shoes when I waved."
items.markingKey: A. The action lets readers infer embarrassment.

items.stem: Explain why writers often show a character's feelings through actions rather than stating them.
items.answer: Showing invites readers to infer and makes characters feel real; readers become more involved when they work out feelings themselves.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Showing invites readers to infer and makes characters feel real; readers become more involved when they work out feelings themselves. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between indirect characterisation and direct characterisation.
items.answer: Direct characterisation tells the reader what a character is like ("She was brave"); indirect characterisation shows it through speech, actions and thoughts, so the reader infers it.
items.markingKey: Direct characterisation tells the reader what a character is like ("She was brave"); indirect characterisation shows it through speech, actions and thoughts, so the reader infers it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If a character says they are fine, the reader should believe them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Characters can hide feelings; their actions or the narrator's details may contradict their words, and readers should look for these clues.
items.markingKey: Characters can hide feelings; their actions or the narrator's details may contradict their words, and readers should look for these clues. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Read this sentence: "Oliver told his mum he had loads of friends. It was easier than the truth." What can you infer about Oliver? Give one reason.
items.answer: He is lonely (he has few or no friends) and wants to protect his mum from worrying; "easier than the truth" shows he hides his feelings.
items.markingKey: He is lonely (he has few or no friends) and wants to protect his mum from worrying; "easier than the truth" shows he hides his feelings.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about a boy who eats lunch alone.

Every lunchtime Oliver ate on the bench behind the music block, where the wind smelled of old leaves and nobody came.
He told his mum he had loads of friends. It was easier than the truth.
On Tuesday, a tuba case appeared at the other end of the bench, followed by a tall girl with a sandwich.
"Is this your bench?" she asked.
"It's nobody's bench," Oliver said.
"Good," said the girl, sitting down. "Then it can be ours."

Explain what the character's actions and words reveal about them.
items.answer: Oliver is lonely and hides it to protect his mother ("It was easier than the truth"); the girl is confident and friendly, turning his phrase "nobody's bench" into an invitation.
items.markingKey: Oliver is lonely and hides it to protect his mother ("It was easier than the truth"); the girl is confident and friendly, turning his phrase "nobody's bench" into an invitation. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Choose a character from a novel you have studied. Explain how the writer reveals their personality through actions, speech and thoughts, with one quotation for each.
items.answer: Indicative content: three methods with a short quotation each; inference about personality; effect on the reader. Criterion A and B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: three methods with a short quotation each; inference about personality; effect on the reader. Criterion A and B.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about a boy who eats lunch alone.

Every lunchtime Oliver ate on the bench behind the music block, where the wind smelled of old leaves and nobody came.
He told his mum he had loads of friends. It was easier than the truth.
On Tuesday, a tuba case appeared at the other end of the bench, followed by a tall girl with a sandwich.
"Is this your bench?" she asked.
"It's nobody's bench," Oliver said.
"Good," said the girl, sitting down. "Then it can be ours."

How does the writer show the beginning of a friendship in this extract?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The setting ("where the wind smelled of old leaves and nobody came") reflects Oliver's loneliness, and his lie to his mum shows how hidden it is. The arrival of the tuba case breaks the routine, and the girl's wordplay ("Then it can be ours") turns his lonely phrase into an invitation, showing belonging can begin with a small act of welcome.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The setting ("where the wind smelled of old leaves and nobody came") reflects Oliver's loneliness, and his lie to his mum shows how hidden it is. The arrival of the tuba case breaks the routine, and the girl's wordplay ("Then it can be ours") turns his lonely phrase into an invitation, showing belonging can begin with a small act of welcome. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "third-person narration"?
options: An analytical paragraph that makes a Point, gives Evidence (a quotation) and Explains how the evidence supports the point
A story told by a narrator outside the action using "he", "she" and "they"
A novel in which different characters take turns to tell the story, giving different points of view
The first sentence of a paragraph, which states its main point
items.answer: A story told by a narrator outside the action using "he", "she" and "they"
items.markingKey: B. "third-person narration" is a story told by a narrator outside the action using "he", "she" and "they".

items.stem: Explain the difference between first-person narration and third-person narration.
items.answer: First-person narration ("I") gives one character's inner view and voice; third-person narration ("he/she") comes from outside and may show one or several characters' thoughts with more distance.
items.markingKey: First-person narration ("I") gives one character's inner view and voice; third-person narration ("he/she") comes from outside and may show one or several characters' thoughts with more distance. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a first-person narrator may not give the full truth about other characters.
items.answer: They only see others from the outside and may be biased by their own feelings, so readers must infer what others really think. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They only see others from the outside and may be biased by their own feelings, so readers must infer what others really think. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji writes: "A first-person narrator is always the author." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The narrator is a character created by the author; their views, age and experiences may be very different from the author's.
items.markingKey: The narrator is a character created by the author; their views, age and experiences may be very different from the author's. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in the first person: "Mei stood at the door, her cheeks burning."
items.answer: "I stood at the door, my cheeks burning."
items.markingKey: "I stood at the door, my cheeks burning."

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "First-person narration is the best way to make readers care about a character."
items.answer: First person creates strong intimacy, but third-person limited can be equally powerful while allowing wider perspective; the best choice depends on the story.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives direct access to feelings; the voice feels personal and honest. Arguments against: third-person can show several characters and more context; a limited view may confuse readers. Supported judgement: First person creates strong intimacy, but third-person limited can be equally powerful while allowing wider perspective; the best choice depends on the story.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

Identify the device in the quotation "Twenty-eight faces turned.".
options: rhetorical question
short sentence
personification
simile
items.answer: short sentence
items.markingKey: B. "Twenty-eight faces turned." is an example of short sentence: the brief sentence captures the sudden, overwhelming attention Mei feels.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "theme".
items.answer: A central idea or message explored in a text, such as friendship, belonging or growing up
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a central idea or message explored in a text, such as friendship, belonging or growing up. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a theme and a moral.
items.answer: A theme is an idea a text explores, often with complexity; a moral is a direct lesson the reader is told to learn, as in a fable.
items.markingKey: A theme is an idea a text explores, often with complexity; a moral is a direct lesson the reader is told to learn, as in a fable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why it is better to write a theme as a statement rather than a single word.
items.answer: A single word ("friendship") only names a topic; a statement ("friendships can change painfully as we grow up") shows what the text says about it. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single word ("friendship") only names a topic; a statement ("friendships can change painfully as we grow up") shows what the text says about it. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A story can only have one theme." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most stories explore several connected themes, such as friendship, identity and growing up.
items.markingKey: Most stories explore several connected themes, such as friendship, identity and growing up. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a theme statement (one sentence) for a story about a new student who finds a friend through a shared hobby.
items.answer: For example: "Shared interests can help people overcome loneliness and feel they belong." 1 mark for a statement, 1 for relevance.
items.markingKey: For example: "Shared interests can help people overcome loneliness and feel they belong." 1 mark for a statement, 1 for relevance.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The theme of a novel is whatever the reader thinks it is."
items.answer: Readers can find different themes, but a convincing theme must be supported by evidence from the text.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: readers bring their own experiences; many themes can be valid. Arguments against: interpretations must be supported by evidence in the text; the writer's choices guide meaning. Supported judgement: Readers can find different themes, but a convincing theme must be supported by evidence from the text.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is better to write a theme as a statement rather than a single word.

items.stem: Which sentence is the best "Point" for a PEE paragraph about Mei?
items.answer: The writer presents Mei as anxious on her first day.
items.markingKey: The writer presents Mei as anxious on her first day.. A point is an arguable claim about the text.

items.stem: Briefly explain why short quotations are usually better than long ones.
items.answer: Short, precise quotations focus on the exact words being analysed and can be embedded smoothly, showing close reading.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Short, precise quotations focus on the exact words being analysed and can be embedded smoothly, showing close reading. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between explanation and evidence.
items.answer: Evidence is the quotation or reference from the text; explanation is the writer's own analysis of what the evidence shows and how it affects the reader.
items.markingKey: Evidence is the quotation or reference from the text; explanation is the writer's own analysis of what the evidence shows and how it affects the reader. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write a PEE paragraph about how the writer presents Thabo in the missing-dog story, using the quotation "He thought about his mother's empty purse."
items.answer: Point: Thabo is tempted by the reward because his family is poor. Evidence: the quotation. Explanation: the image of the "empty purse" shows financial need, making his kind choice more meaningful. Criteria A and B.
items.markingKey: Point: Thabo is tempted by the reward because his family is poor. Evidence: the quotation. Explanation: the image of the "empty purse" shows financial need, making his kind choice more meaningful. Criteria A and B.

items.stem: A student claims: "The more quotations you include, the better your paragraph." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: One or two well-chosen, well-explained quotations are better than many unexplained ones.
items.markingKey: One or two well-chosen, well-explained quotations are better than many unexplained ones. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel told by two narrators.

AMARA
When the new boy sat in my seat on the bus, I didn't say anything. I just glared. He didn't even notice. Typical.

TOMÁS
I sat in the only empty seat. A girl glared at me like I'd stolen her kidney. I wanted to say sorry, but my English comes out wrong when I'm nervous, so I looked out of the window and counted lamp posts until my stop. Forty-three.

Explain, in point-evidence-explanation form, why the writer uses the minor sentence "Typical.".
items.answer: Minor sentence: "Typical." – the one-word judgement reveals Amara's quick assumption about the new boy.
items.markingKey: Minor sentence: "Typical." – the one-word judgement reveals Amara's quick assumption about the new boy. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The PEE structure makes all student writing sound the same."
items.answer: PEE is a useful foundation, especially in MYP 3, but writers should develop it by embedding evidence and linking ideas.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it can become formulaic; strong writers vary their structure. Arguments against: it guarantees evidence and explanation; it is a foundation that can be developed (PEEL, extended explanation). Supported judgement: PEE is a useful foundation, especially in MYP 3, but writers should develop it by embedding evidence and linking ideas.

items.stem:
Read the following free verse poem by a student poet, "Lagos at Midnight".

The city does not sleep;
it hums,
a generator heart
beating under every street.
Danfo buses honk like geese.
A radio somewhere
is singing to nobody,
and the moon,
tired of competing,
hides behind the billboards.

Write two linked PEE paragraphs (about 250 words) that answer: How does the poet use imagery and sound to present Lagos at night?
items.answer: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "inference"?
options: When the narrator tells the reader directly what a character is like (e.g. "She was shy")
An object, person or place that represents a bigger idea (e.g. a faded sign representing a fading friendship)
A conclusion the reader works out from clues in the text, rather than from something stated directly
A story told by a character using "I", so the reader sees events through that character's eyes
items.answer: A conclusion the reader works out from clues in the text, rather than from something stated directly
items.markingKey: C. "inference" is a conclusion the reader works out from clues in the text, rather than from something stated directly.

items.stem: What should the Explanation in a PEE paragraph do?
options: Explain how the evidence supports the point and its effect on the reader
Repeat the quotation
Give the page number only
Retell the next event
items.answer: Explain how the evidence supports the point and its effect on the reader
items.markingKey: A. Explanation is where analysis happens.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel told by two narrators.

AMARA
When the new boy sat in my seat on the bus, I didn't say anything. I just glared. He didn't even notice. Typical.

TOMÁS
I sat in the only empty seat. A girl glared at me like I'd stolen her kidney. I wanted to say sorry, but my English comes out wrong when I'm nervous, so I looked out of the window and counted lamp posts until my stop. Forty-three.

Why might the writer have chosen this narrative voice? Refer to the text.
items.answer: Two first-person narrators give the same event from different sides: Amara thinks Tomás is rude ("He didn't even notice"), but Tomás reveals he did notice and was too nervous to speak. The reader knows more than either character (dramatic irony).
items.markingKey: Two first-person narrators give the same event from different sides: Amara thinks Tomás is rude ("He didn't even notice"), but Tomás reveals he did notice and was too nervous to speak. The reader knows more than either character (dramatic irony). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.answer: Most stories explore several connected themes, such as friendship, identity and growing up.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a first-person novel about two friends.

Dev and I built the treehouse the summer we were ten. We nailed a sign to it: NO GROWN-UPS. NO GIRLS. NO EXCEPTIONS.
Now we're thirteen and the sign is still there, faded and crooked, and Dev hasn't climbed up for months.
Today I saw him at the bus stop with Marcus's crowd. He laughed at something Marcus said. I waved. He looked at his shoes.
I went home and climbed the ladder alone. I took the sign down. Then I put it back up. I don't know why.

What does "crooked" suggest here? Explain the connotations of the word in context.
items.answer: "crooked" means not straight; bent or twisted here; it suggests the friendship is now damaged and out of shape.
items.markingKey: "crooked" means not straight; bent or twisted here; it suggests the friendship is now damaged and out of shape. 1 mark for the meaning in context; further marks for connotation and effect.

items.stem: A student claims: "A PEE paragraph is complete once you have included a quotation." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The quotation must be explained: the analysis of word choice and effect is what earns marks.
items.markingKey: The quotation must be explained: the analysis of word choice and effect is what earns marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a writer might choose first-person narration for a story about friendship.
items.answer: It lets readers share the narrator's private feelings (hurt, loyalty, confusion) directly, creating sympathy and intimacy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It lets readers share the narrator's private feelings (hurt, loyalty, confusion) directly, creating sympathy and intimacy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a moral and a theme.
items.answer: A theme is an idea a text explores, often with complexity; a moral is a direct lesson the reader is told to learn, as in a fable.
items.markingKey: A theme is an idea a text explores, often with complexity; a moral is a direct lesson the reader is told to learn, as in a fable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "If a character says they are fine, the reader should believe them." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Characters can hide feelings; their actions or the narrator's details may contradict their words, and readers should look for these clues.
items.markingKey: Characters can hide feelings; their actions or the narrator's details may contradict their words, and readers should look for these clues. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why retelling the story is not the same as analysing it.
items.answer: Retelling describes what happens; analysis explains how the writer's choices (words, structure, techniques) create meaning and affect the reader.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Retelling describes what happens; analysis explains how the writer's choices (words, structure, techniques) create meaning and affect the reader. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how multiple narrators can create dramatic irony.
items.answer: When each narrator reveals private thoughts, the reader knows things the other characters do not, so we watch misunderstandings unfold.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When each narrator reveals private thoughts, the reader knows things the other characters do not, so we watch misunderstandings unfold. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel told by two narrators.

AMARA
When the new boy sat in my seat on the bus, I didn't say anything. I just glared. He didn't even notice. Typical.

TOMÁS
I sat in the only empty seat. A girl glared at me like I'd stolen her kidney. I wanted to say sorry, but my English comes out wrong when I'm nervous, so I looked out of the window and counted lamp posts until my stop. Forty-three.

Identify a theme of this extract and explain how it is developed.
items.answer: Theme: misunderstanding and seeing others' perspectives. How it is developed: Amara's section shows her judgement ("He didn't even notice. Typical."), but Tomás's section reveals the opposite: he noticed the glare ("like I'd stolen her kidney") and wanted to apologise but was too nervous. Switching narrators creates dramatic irony, so the reader understands both sides, and the detail of counting lamp posts builds sympathy for Tomás.
items.markingKey: Theme: misunderstanding and seeing others' perspectives. How it is developed: Amara's section shows her judgement ("He didn't even notice. Typical."), but Tomás's section reveals the opposite: he noticed the glare ("like I'd stolen her kidney") and wanted to apologise but was too nervous. Switching narrators creates dramatic irony, so the reader understands both sides, and the detail of counting lamp posts builds sympathy for Tomás. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: "The more quotations you include, the better your paragraph." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: One or two well-chosen, well-explained quotations are better than many unexplained ones.
items.markingKey: One or two well-chosen, well-explained quotations are better than many unexplained ones. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Rewrite this first-person sentence in the third person: "I waved, but he looked at his shoes."
items.answer: "He waved, but Dev looked at his shoes." (or "The narrator waved..."). Any correct third-person version.
items.markingKey: "He waved, but Dev looked at his shoes." (or "The narrator waved..."). Any correct third-person version.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a first-person novel about two friends.

Dev and I built the treehouse the summer we were ten. We nailed a sign to it: NO GROWN-UPS. NO GIRLS. NO EXCEPTIONS.
Now we're thirteen and the sign is still there, faded and crooked, and Dev hasn't climbed up for months.
Today I saw him at the bus stop with Marcus's crowd. He laughed at something Marcus said. I waved. He looked at his shoes.
I went home and climbed the ladder alone. I took the sign down. Then I put it back up. I don't know why.

Analyse the effect of the time shift from "the summer we were ten" to "Now we're thirteen" in the text.
items.answer: The time shift from "the summer we were ten" to "Now we're thirteen": the contrast between past and present shows how much the friendship has changed.
items.markingKey: The time shift from "the summer we were ten" to "Now we're thirteen": the contrast between past and present shows how much the friendship has changed. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a first-person novel about two friends.

Dev and I built the treehouse the summer we were ten. We nailed a sign to it: NO GROWN-UPS. NO GIRLS. NO EXCEPTIONS.
Now we're thirteen and the sign is still there, faded and crooked, and Dev hasn't climbed up for months.
Today I saw him at the bus stop with Marcus's crowd. He laughed at something Marcus said. I waved. He looked at his shoes.
I went home and climbed the ladder alone. I took the sign down. Then I put it back up. I don't know why.

How does the writer present the narrator's feelings about his changing friendship with Dev?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: Point: the narrator is hurt but unwilling to let go. Evidence: "I waved. He looked at his shoes." Explanation: the short, flat sentences present the rejection without comment, making the hurt more powerful. The faded, crooked sign symbolises the damaged friendship, and the contradictory actions ("I took the sign down. Then I put it back up.") and the honest "I don't know why" show mixed feelings of loss and hope.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Point: the narrator is hurt but unwilling to let go. Evidence: "I waved. He looked at his shoes." Explanation: the short, flat sentences present the rejection without comment, making the hurt more powerful. The faded, crooked sign symbolises the damaged friendship, and the contradictory actions ("I took the sign down. Then I put it back up.") and the honest "I don't know why" show mixed feelings of loss and hope. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "The PEE structure makes all student writing sound the same." Discuss.
items.answer: PEE is a useful foundation, especially in MYP 3, but writers should develop it by embedding evidence and linking ideas.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it can become formulaic; strong writers vary their structure. Arguments against: it guarantees evidence and explanation; it is a foundation that can be developed (PEEL, extended explanation). Supported judgement: PEE is a useful foundation, especially in MYP 3, but writers should develop it by embedding evidence and linking ideas. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a first-person novel about two friends.

Dev and I built the treehouse the summer we were ten. We nailed a sign to it: NO GROWN-UPS. NO GIRLS. NO EXCEPTIONS.
Now we're thirteen and the sign is still there, faded and crooked, and Dev hasn't climbed up for months.
Today I saw him at the bus stop with Marcus's crowd. He laughed at something Marcus said. I waved. He looked at his shoes.
I went home and climbed the ladder alone. I took the sign down. Then I put it back up. I don't know why.

Rewrite the bus-stop scene (about 200 words) from Dev's point of view, showing why he looked at his shoes.
items.answer: Indicative content: first person as Dev; consistent events (Marcus's crowd, the wave); inner conflict between wanting to fit in and guilt; realistic dialogue or thoughts; a hint about the treehouse.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: first person as Dev; consistent events (Marcus's crowd, the wave); inner conflict between wanting to fit in and guilt; realistic dialogue or thoughts; a hint about the treehouse. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).
